title: Food-tracking salience can change feeding habits and dietary diversity, but not food quantity or child nutrition status by itself
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11461, Food Accounting Salience and Dietary Diversity: A Randomized Impact Evaluation of an Intervention to Track and Improve Young Children's Food Consumption in Bihar, India
geography: 2,682 households with children aged 6–24 months across six districts of Bihar, India, in a cluster-randomized intervention delivered with frontline-worker support

observations.period: December 2022-July 2023 intervention and follow-up; cluster-randomized trial

denominator.unit: households with children aged 6–24 months in six Bihar districts

intervention.value: mothers in treatment households received a wall-mounted food-tracking journal

attention.value: the intervention increased mothers' attention to and automaticity of key feeding behaviors

dietary_diversity.value: the intervention increased the probability that children achieved minimum dietary diversity

behavioral_route.value: salience and tracking can reinforce reminders and habit formation around feeding

observations.method: Cluster-randomized controlled trial of a household-level wall-journal intervention, with feeding behavior, beliefs, and child dietary outcomes measured over follow-up.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates are specific to the Bihar households, child ages, journal design, frontline-worker delivery, food environment, and study period; the result does not establish identical effects in other nutrition settings.
observations.subgroup: Mothers and caregivers of young children, children with different feeding needs, households with different food access and income, and frontline workers delivering the intervention.
observations.counterinterpretation: The journal may operate through contact with the frontline worker, attention from the research encounter, or social desirability rather than the physical tracking tool alone.

observations.period: Five months post-treatment; child quantity and anthropometric outcomes

denominator.unit: randomized Bihar households and children in the study frame

food_quantity.value: no detectable change in the quantity of food fed to children

child_muac.value: no detectable change in children's mid-upper arm circumference

persistence.value: changes in food diversity were small five months after treatment

constraint.value: food availability and household income limited improvements in dietary diversity

observations.method: Randomized follow-up comparison of feeding quantity, dietary diversity, and child anthropometric status.
observations.uncertainty: The study period and outcomes do not establish long-run growth, health, food security, or whether larger complementary investments would amplify the behavioral effect.
observations.subgroup: Households with different incomes, food availability, market access, seasonal exposure, and children at different nutritional risk.
observations.counterinterpretation: Anthropometric measures may require longer follow-up or stronger dietary changes; a null quantity effect does not mean the intervention had no welfare value.

observations.period: 2026 paper; delivery heterogeneity and household economic status

denominator.unit: Bihar randomized households with frontline-worker delivery and economic-status comparisons

frontline_worker.value: impacts varied by the frontline worker delivering the intervention

economic_status.value: better-off households showed larger gains in knowledge, perceived norms, and habit formation

dietary_effect.value: treatment effects on dietary diversity did not differ by household economic status

system_route.value: behavior tools work through a delivery relationship and within material constraints, not as stand-alone information

observations.method: Cluster-randomized intervention analysis with frontline-worker and household-economic-status heterogeneity.
observations.uncertainty: The heterogeneity findings do not identify all worker characteristics, household mechanisms, or long-run equity effects, and do not prove that the intervention equalizes nutrition outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Frontline workers, mothers, poorer and better-off households, children with different food access, and local nutrition systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Worker variation may reflect caseload, geography, trust, language, supervision, or measurement differences; economic-status patterns can differ for outcomes not measured here.

related_sources.claim: Abstract and bibliographic record for World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11461.
World Bank reproducibility package with trial design, data description, and computational verification metadata.
Related World Bank Bihar nutrition impact-evaluation data and intervention context.

boundary: This record adds a causal salience-and-tracking-to-feeding-behavior and dietary-diversity route, with explicit limits around food quantity, child MUAC, persistence, income and food availability, frontline-worker delivery, and household heterogeneity. It does not establish long-run nutrition or growth effects, food-security improvement, universal transferability, or that behavior tools can substitute for affordable diverse food and reliable care infrastructure.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank working-paper PDF, abstract, reproducibility package, and related data record were reviewed for the 2,682-household cluster RCT, wall-journal intervention, behavior and dietary-diversity effects, null food-quantity and MUAC outcomes, five-month boundary, frontline-worker variation, and income/food-availability constraints.
